May 5 of 1992, id Software released Wolfenstein 3D. Its a revolution, a new era. Some critics call it "The Godfather of FPS 3D games". One year later Doom would be launched & four years after Quake & Duke Nukem 3D, to mention the pioneers of the genre.
I played in my childhood Wolfenstein trilogy: Wolf 3D, Spear of Destinity & nine years later Return to Castle Wolfenstein. I was big fan of this series when I was a kid, afterwards I missed 2009 Wolfenstein, so at the beginning of this game I had very high pretensions of what I expected, due to the love for the old saga.
From where start... Superb, fantastical, magnificent, marvellous... again as at 1992 I got stunned. 
With the reservation that this game was released almost 5 years ago and also that I have not played the biggest titles released in the last 5 years either, I felt again that I was playing to another thing, a new revolution.
The diesel its fantastic, its feels great.
In fact, all is great with this game: graphics, in-game sounds, soundtrack, history, artwork, gameplay, everything. The ambiance is incredible.
Lets talk a bit about history. You are on 60s & Nazis win WW2, then a parallel reality is drawn who has lots of references to what happened in that decade. Some examples: on 60s US reached the moon, not in this case, it was the Nazis which also was capable to build Gibraltar Bridge. The are also several references to musicians & intellectuals from that decade. Through newspaper clippings and small details you can find more references, some of them proper to history. You can even hear some vinyl-sounding releases of the time, ofc they aint about The Beatles & The Animals, instead there are parallel records of these artist, recorded in german. Yes, so you can hear House of The Rising Sun on german. F@cking Jimmy Hendrix is at this game man! You also can remember old memories & play one short level at Wolf 3D.
Lets talk about level design now, Wolfenstein what you do spect? Castle, open doors & kill nazis? Nope.
The game is versatile to the maximum, all levels are different. Where you want action?
some WW2, play at D day? check Airplane? check Chopper? check, Train? check, Submarine? check, Sea? check, Vault? check, Mental asylum? check, Prison? check, Catacombs? check . check check check I can go on but I don't want spoil any more.
Gameplay: You decide how you play. You like stealth? Play as silent assasin, you don't have Hitman's garrote & Silverballs but you have knifes & silenced pistol. You like tactic gameplay? Study the field and prepare ambushes, R6 style, with a cover system that works splendidly unlike other titles. You like assault, Serious Sam style? Go ahead, grab a gun in each hand and kill them all. All these mechanics are all solid and well-designed. Polish is perfect aswell.
There is so much love put on this game, so much dedication, so many bit tiny details, that's why we love Bethesda.
But after they go & buy id Software and they fire everyone, that's why we hate Bethesda.
I almost forgot, optimizition? Works perfect I ran game without any problem on my old PC.
Weapon & customizations, voices, well, I can go on for an hour writing, everything is very good at this game, as I see.

This is such a good game. Interesting story and situation with great graphics. Theres humor, sex and nazis. I was a bit worried this would be too futuristic for me, but Nope! Its just perfect, definitely recommended 8)

During the development of the new Wolf - I was skeptical. Hell, up until release I was skeptical. I feared they were going to CoDify my beloved Wolf and BJ Blazkowicz would never again be the baddest Nazi-killin motherfucker this side of the 4th Reich. 

But I was wrong. 

Although it starts out slow - Wolfenstein: TNO soon turns into one hell of a game. It looks as good as any modern shooter, plays like the mid 2000's shooters like Soldier of Fortune you remember so well, and tells a story so ridiculous yet so deathly serious you can't help but get caught up in it. Not to mention the characters. Hell, it's been weeks since I beat this game and I can still name all the main characters in this story without hardly even thinking about it. They're all so well realized. So well voiced. They're all important. It's a rare thing in shooters these days.  But it all comes back to Blazko: 

One part Lt. Aldo Raine, two parts John McClane and three parts Bear Jew. BJ is back and a better character than he has ever been. Simply put, he IS the baddest Nazi Killin' motherfucker you've ever met. And he's not going down without a fight. Or two. Or three. Or ten. In fact, over the 12-15 hours it'll take you to beat this single player only affair, you'll ask yourself repeatedly - how is this grizzled old fuck not dead yet?! "Get up, old man. You ain't done yet."

Machinegames did a hell of a job bringing Wolf back for a new generation and as an old school Wolf fan and a champion of old school shooters, I can't say enough about Wolfenstein: TNO. Hell, the best compliment I could give it is that this is the sort of game Raven wishes they could still be making. Equal parts emotional, cinematic, bloody and badass. It's a 2014 FPS ripped right out of 2004's FPS style. You know, back when games like Half Life 2 were what we played, and Call of Duty single player campaigns still meant something.

What else can I say? Get it. And get to killin' some fuckin' Nazis.

Kinda crazy to think that "killing Nazis is a good thing, actually" is a hot take these days, but here we are. Reminder that killing a Nazi isn't murder. It's just taking out the trash.

Side note that the graphics haven't aged super great, but the experience is overall enjoyable.

If you're reading this, that means you've thought about getting into the Wolfenstein series, and this is the perfect place to be for that. I'll be reviewing the game specifically for someone who is just considering playing it, and in separate sections. It will contain no spoilers. I hope you find it useful!

[LORE]
Nazi Germany has won the most deadliest war in human history thanks to an ancient technology and science that is found and twisted by them in order to help the total war effort, most notably, by General Deathshead. This Nazi-controlled world shows the extremes of inhumane brutality, ruthlessness, ugliness and absolute power. It's scary. You, as William Joseph Blazkowicz can't tolerate that. There is still hope, there is bound to be people that are against this tyranny and willing to fight and resist it. So the fight continues, this time not to win an ideology or land or material, but to win freedom.
There are themes of George Orwell's 1984, so if you're fan of that novel, you will very much like the lore and world of Wolfenstein as well. If you like the lore of games like DOOM, Dead Space, Middle Earth series or games alike, you will most likely enjoy Wolfenstein too due to the similarity in the theme of resisting and fighting a powerful evil while being outnumbered. This is a game about hope. About resistance. About humanity. 

[GAMEPLAY]
Incredibly rich, FPS, story driven game filled with neat gameplay mechanics that is also immersive. You're a one man army, kill all the Nazis in various ways and explore a variety of weapons, tools, places, difficulties, enemies, obstacles, horrors and whatnot to achieve your goals. Get creative, get angry and transfer that energy into your weapons.
Relatively easy and usually dumb stealth, but very enjoyable and rewarding.
Beautiful mission designs. The type that has you actively thinking about it, wondering what's right and what's not, exploring possibilities, failing, trying again better next time, developing your own preferred style of killing Nazis.
Very nice animations and movement. Can't get tired of it. 
Once again, if you're a fan of DOOM's gameplay, you will most definitely like this gameplay as well, even though there are naturally some big differences. Other games like Metro, Prey, Dishonored resemble this type of gameplay to some degree.

[GRAPHICS AND OPTIMIZATION]
Artistic, beautiful graphics. It's not ultra realistic and it's not underdeveloped either. It's like a painting, it's truly artistic realistic with nice details. Optimization is really good as well. I've never experienced even a single stutter or hardware problem playing this game, and I believe it should run pretty well on most devices. I had to use VSync because of the constant screen tearing I experienced without it, and that is definitely a complaint, but not that much of a big deal for me. I got used to VSync's delay quite quickly. 

[LENGTH]
Medium length. It took me about 9 hours to complete on ÜBER difficulty, and I didn't try to get all the secrets and upgrades, but I did certainly pay attention to all the details and looked for as much secrets and upgrades as I thought reasonable, so it's fair to say I didn't rush the game. All and all, I think it can take somewhere between 6 to 12 hours to complete, depending on how you play and how good you are at the game.

[AUDIO AND SOUNDTRACK]
Neat. It's Mick Gordon on the soundtrack and that is enough to say about it, but besides the music, everything else about the audio, the voice actors, the sound quality, etc is absolutely amazing. It's original, it's special, it's Wolfenstein. 

[GOLD BARS]
Nicely priced. It gets nice discounts too, so you might want to wait a little while if you don't want to pay the original price.

[BUGS]
I did not encounter any significant bug to mention here. Clean game.

[RATING]
A gem in all of gaming. The type of game that you can talk about for hours and not get tired of it. The type of game that surpassed the original standards. Maybe not revolutionary, but surely memorable and worthy of respect. 
9.5/10

[TIPS]
1. spend some time in the hideout. Discover secrets, help people in need, interact with people and things, listen to conversations, read the newspapers, address the details and enjoy them. It makes the game all the more interesting in my opinion.

2. After you kill a super soldier, shoot off the armor plates using its own MG60. There you have it, free extra armor for your next encounter of whatever atrocity they throw at you.

3. Fergus, Wyatt, doesn't matter. In the end, you will think either decision was a mistake.
In real world where social media owning scumbags throw up Nazi salutes, play this fantastic game where you can give them the good ol' G.I. Robot treatment.

If you played the first level - you will get that old Wolfenstein feeling back. And to be fair - no, its NOT that fun, It can be overwhelming to be thrown into the action from the start, and a bit exhausting cause "here we are again", killing Nazis and blowing up everything in our way. The real New Order actually starts after that level. And that depth hasn't been seen in old Wolfie games at all. You will start to care for the story (it still is about Nazis dominating the world but hey you cant change that premise), you will develop the interest for the people around you, you will start to notice all the little pieces of information thrown around the levels, and you will see the narrative of the game going only upwards. Right until the end. And what an ending it is.

The New Order tried and succeded  to tell us a story. It still is crazy fun to shoot and kill, but this time - it seems like there really is a bigger purpose. Shooting is great, stealth has its ups and downs, but overall - the flow is just right. One of the most overlooked games. Big recommendation.

I have been a fan of Wolfenstein since the original and I was hoping beyond reason that the latest incarnation of this single player first person shooter classic did the franchise justice. And it did that and then some. It went back to the basics, polished them up, and delivered one of the best games I have played in a long time.

This game is a single player FPS in its purest form. Lots of enemies, lots of weapons and lots of different viable ways to play. It has a great mix of stealth, tactical shooting and all out, in your face, duel auto-shotgun wiedling, death dealing mayhem. It manages to make killing Nazis a lot of fun, and manages to keep it fun throughout the whole game.

Not for the squeemish and not for those who object to people killing Nazis. But for any single player first person shooter gamer, this is a must have game.

Update 5/21: My system specs are as follows: Intel i5 2500K @ 3.3GHZ, 32 GB sys ram, 1TB HDD, Windows 8.1, Nvdida Drivers 335.23 ( I know they aren't the latest drivers, but I don't upgrade my drivers until I have trouble playing a game because  I've found sometimes new drivers can cause problems with games that were working fine).

This is a solid title. No doubts about it. The rumors about the AI being poor don't hold up to what I've experienced so far. Enemies will take cover, duck out to take shots, roll to make themselves harder targets, and commanders will even continuously call in reinforcements until they are killed. I started at "Hard" difficulty and it feels like the right setting for veteran gamers. One potential issue that can make the game easier is that there is a bit of overabundance in terms of medkits and armor for my taste. Every time you clear an area, you'll find that there are significant numbers of health, ammo, and armor picks-up scattered all around. Of course, you can be as judicious as you like in terms of how many you take, but they could have scaled back on the amount of pick-up a bit. 

The visuals are generally very solid, with the occasional glitch here and there, and the framerate is smooth and steady. The only complaint I have in this regard is that there is still random screen tearing, even with V-Sync enabled, but it's rare, and hasn't really significantly impacted my experience. I have a GTX 660 with 32 gigs of system RAM. 

I am still early on, but man does this game have atmosphere and some of the best voice acting I have experienced yet. And the cutscenes are quite well done.

The guns are fun so far, but I haven't yet really got anything exotic.  We'll see how that turns out with additional game time, though. 

At any rate, the short of it is get this game if you enjoy FPSs. I am having some really good fun with this one, and I'm about to get back to it now! I'll update this review as needed. 

Cheers!

Update 5/20: I am about 12-13 hours in now, and my initial impressions still hold. This game is a generally solid FPS experience. There's nothing revolutionary here, but it does what it does well. I forgot to mention that you can earn perks as you progress through the game, and the perks are aligned with different playstyles. For example, there is a perk line for stealth that allows you to increase some of the stealth actions at your disposal (i.e. throwing knives) or to improve upon them (i.e. reduce the amount of noise you make when you sprint). Also, all projectile weapons have alternate fire modes , but you have to unlock them through gameplay. I still recommend veteran gamers starting on at least "Hard".

Update 6/3/14: This update is about the weapons, now that I have had a chance to really sink my teeth in the game. There is some variety to be had here in terms of weapons, but you won't see the more exotic weapons (i.e. laser rifles) until much later on in the game. This could be an issue for those of us who are "gun bunnies", and want access sooner rather than later, but I wouldn't let that put you off from what is really a great game. You do get some incremental upgrades to the primary stable of weapons you have access to early on, which include (but are not limited to) the usual suspects like an assault rifle, shotgun, and pistols (which can be actively silenced at will). One such incremental improvement is the addition of a grenade launcher to the standard assault rifle. So, it's not a new weapon, but it definitely adds some additional punch to your damage output, not the mention the fun factor when you want to turn up the heat.

I should also note here that you can dual-wield most of your weapons, and, though I take the stealth route for the most part, I have had some solid fun with full-on assualts while dual-wielding shotguns and assualt rifles.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game with a story that begins in 1946, then fast-forwards to 1960. The Nazis won the war in 1946, the Allies lost, so that Nazis have taken over the world. The introduction to the narrative is long enough that it takes a long time for B.J. Blazkowicz, the main protagonist of the Wolfenstein series, to carry firearms. Mr. Blazkowicz fought in the war for the U.S., but was wounded and spends time in a Polish mental institution in a vegetative state until 1960.

This game is a continuation of the famous Wolfenstein series that has no shame in allowing you to kill as many Nazis as possible. Cities like Berlin and London are now occupied by Nazis as technological terrors such as large mechs and robotic dogs patrol the streets. There are many propaganda posters strewn throughout Germany and London, England making it clear that the Nazis are ruling and that citizens who violate their laws will be severely punished. Mr. Blazkowicz is the man who will take on the Nazis with some help from NPCs who will advise him on where to go and what objectives to complete. Killing Nazis is in his DNA.

The narrative requires you to choose one of two paths that will be slightly different from each other based on which two comrades will die at the hands of evil General Deathshead, the leader of the Nazis. Deathshead kills one of the two comrades you choose for death so that he can use him in an evil experiment that he says will change the world for the better. You will then have to play the game based on the survivor’s timeline. This ability to choose may be cruel, but it adds replayability to the game by encouraging you to play the game twice so that you can experiences both timelines that result in slightly different versions of the narrative.

The gameplay is pretty much an old school FPS. The weapons in the game are not innovative, but they still feel very satisfying and have alternate modes. The run –of-the-mill weapons include handguns, assault rifles, shotguns, and sniper rifles. Each aforementioned weapon can be upgraded and the upgrades will be necessary to take on the bigger and more powerful Nazis. Assault rifles feel powerful when dual wielding them and can be upgraded by acquiring the rocket upgrade. There are perks in the game that you can keep track of that Mr. Blazkowicz can acquire throughout the game to improve the stealth, tactical, assault, and demolition aspects of combat. These perks add a role-playing like feel to the game. The ability to pick up ammo, weapons, health, and armor feels a like old school FPS.

There are certain locales that seem to encourage stealth. This is when the knife comes in handy, allowing you to slash unsuspecting Nazis from behind. The slashings are truly gory and horrific, but satisfying since it feels like they deserve to be slashed by your blade. Some locales can overwhelm you to death if you don’t use stealth, especially if there are officers stationed there. You can detect signals that alert you to the presence of officers. Officers are capable of calling in reinforcements to overwhelm. Stealthily taking down officers is rewarding as the game’s map will open up and reveals secret items such as enigma codes, letters, and gold items. There are other locales that seem to encourage a shootout with Nazis of different sizes and abilities. Nazis are varied enough in terms of clothing and weapons. Some Nazis are powerful rocket wielding and shotgun wielding foes that will seriously test your FPS skills such as the ability to take cover. The levels are varied enough as they include a prison that you must infiltrate, a lunar base run by Nazis, the city of London filled with swastikas to indicate Nazi dominance, and a base occupied by Mr. Blazkowicz’s friends where he receive objectives. It is interesting to see an alternate perspective of World War II with the Nazis winning the war and dominating the world. They actually landed on the moon before the U.S. could ever land one of its own citizens on the moon.

I have always been of the opinion that characters in games should speak their native language. This game nails it by having Nazis speak German when engaged in combat. It makes the game feel more immersive than if they all spoke the English language in a setting that is German. Some of Blazkowicz’s friends speak German and say a few words in German. I felt like I was truly in Germany when the Nazis spoke German during combat. The A.I. is not always perfect, but it is good enough to test your FPS abilities in the spur of the moment.

One new weapon in the game is the laser cutter known as the laserkraftwerk (LKW). When you first acquire this weapon, it is a utility that can be used to cut holes in metal gratings that block your progress. There are other metal gratings that can be cut for the purpose of finding secret items. Once it is upgraded the LKW becomes more than a utility item: it then contains an alternate mode which is a weapon that is very effective against mechanical enemies. They don’t require ammo since they run on batteries that can be recharged at the various recharge stations.

The graphics look very modern and make the 1992 version of Wolfenstein seem pale in comparison. The cutscenes look polished. The levels look picturesque and very realistic, whether they are in Berlin, Germany or London, England.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is the first game this year I've actively played to completion at every opportunity. It's that good. It's solid, polished and when the gun fights are going down it's magnificent, fluid and testing. The boss fights are testing at points too with audio hints and clues if you get a little stuck working out what to do. The main point to make here is the boss fights are well designed with an old school approach in mind. They require some quick reflexes, fast thinking and a little intelligence/perception to work out what to do. I love this, I really do.

The sound track is like silky smooth milk chocolate to the ears. The music fits the ambience of the levels/scenarios and really gets the adrenaline pumping during gun fights. The sound track changes on the fly depending on how much action is going on at any given time and never seems out of place. It invoked emotion in me. If I made a mistake while taking the stealth option and was forced to bring out the akimbo assault rifles the music adapated fueling my adrenaline and passion for mowing down nazis! MEIN LIEBEN!

AMD FX (Piledriver) 8350 (8 Core) 4Ghz
16gb 1333mhz DDR RAM

I'm 99.9% sure you're going to love it and even be charmed by the little touches which blend modern technology and techniques with properly good old school mechanics which started the genre.

This game is really damn good. And that was unexpected, to me, after all, who expects anything from a Wolfenstein, especially after Wolf 2009? As a sequel-reboot, this game is all parts visceral, gritty, and smart.

Don't pass this up. Play this game.

I've been told to play this game probably ever since it was released, and all I can say after playing it for multiple hours is Extraordinary. What an absolute joy of a shooter. I had a hankering for something big and ugly and satisfying, and hot diggidy daffodil did Wolfenstein deliver. 

The combat is heavy, brutal, and just thrilling. Trading fire with teched-out Nazis never gets boring, and the feeling of plugging these fascist bastards full of lead is pure dumb video game fun. Particularly enjoyed using the throwing knives (very satisfying "ting!" when you get a hit), the machine gun (very good sense of power barely under control), and the silenced luger (accurate, usually a one-hit kill). I was less enamored with fighting most of the robotic enemies, since they were usually thwarted by hitting them with a tesla grenade and plugging them in the back, which gets old. The hybrid robot/human enemies are generally fun to fight, but nothing really comes close to the regular ol' humans.

I really got into the narrative too, which is... look, I was expecting the absolute worst from a Wolfenstein game, story-wise, but wow did they did a fantastic job on it. It's a really cool, really well-realized alternate history of World War 2 where the allies get suddenly and severely out-teched by the Nazis. Just watching how much harder it is for the allies to do anything in the face of such power is interesting, and I loved the prevading attitude of "if you find a Nazi weapon, drop yours and pick it up. It's bound to be better than what we've got." It gets a biiiiiiit ridiculous at the very end? I suppose? But honestly, that turn is done in an entertainingly crazy way, and it doesn't so much jump the shark as treat an absolutely absurd concept completely seriously, which... if they're going to go with it, I'm glad they went all the way with it.

Was also very surprised to find there are actual characters in this game, and well-realized ones at that. The scenes surrounding most of the supporting cast are dramatic without feeling corny, fleshing out regular people living in a pretty crazy universe. I honestly can't think of anyone in this game I did not like, as a character. Again, it's very well done, and it's something I would've never expected from a title like this.

So yeah, I very much recommend playing this through. It's satisfying, it's well-told, it's immersive, and it goes all the way with a concept I would've never expected them to commit to. Very much looking forward to the next game in the series, if it ever happens.

Wolfenstein the new order is an action fps set in an alternate history where the Nazis won the second war. You play as William Blazkowicz and your goal is to destroy this new Nazi world order.

The game can be done in 2 different ways, you can do it by shooting everything that moves or by infiltration. The combat is extremely satisfying, you can double wield, slide, insta kill and throw knives. It's a Nazi massacre with a Doom twist.

Despite of following its ancestors, Wolfenstein: The New Order is not all about shooting Nazis.

It's year 1946. Despite of Allies having advantage over Nazi-Germany, Nazis have turned the tables, thanks to mad scientist called Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse, and the war machines he invented.
Allies have decided to make the final attack against Strasse, and are going to invade his castle.
You, B.J. Blazkowicz, as one of the members of Allies, are going to help at the war front.

The characters are each one of their own kind, you can feel the ways they react, and how they interact with each other.
I absolutely love the fact how characters and story completely took me with them. The more i played, the more i grew respect to the characters, and their backstories, how they lived before war and what made them the people who they are today.
I love how i felt different feelings against different characters, hate, love, pity, sadness. I might have cried tiny manly tears at some point.

Nazis are corrupting the world and the people who live there, one of the best moments without doubt is to revenge with large variety of guns and weapon modifications, for example, automatic shotgun, and assault rifle.
The gameplay part is mostly about shooting, but all the stages contain lots of puzzles, but only few of them are needed to make progress in the game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order has lots of similarities with so-called "old-school games", and with this i mean that you have to collect your own Ammo, Health and Armor throughout the game.
You can stay stealthy in shadows and take out guards without getting detected, or just take over the guns and destroy every living thing on your way. Game does not choose for you, You choose for yourself. I like that.

As you process further, game makes itself harder by adding more enemies. Enemies in the end of the game have lots of armor, do significant amounts of damage, and patrol more actively. Some might say they grow brains.
Need to point out though, how i managed to kill a guard in front of another guard with throwing knife without the other one noticing.

About the replay value; there are lots of in-game collectibles like concept art, gold statues, character bios, upgrades, letters and Enigma codes, which unlock modes to game. For example, Permanent death mode (1 death is game over without continues).

I played through story in about 10 hours with 2nd difficulty. There are 4 difficulties to choose from.
About the bugs and/or glitches, there are some, but on my sessions none of them caused game crashes.

It's a good game and you can get it for fairly cheap for 19,99€ on Steam Store.
About the system requirements though, this might not play on a bit older computers.
I recommend for players who are excited of war-themed games with great story and variety of characters.
And of course, whacking Nazis.

[h1] Wolfenstein new order [/h1]

[b] The Good [/b]
-	Story is more heartfelt than I thought and BJ dialog sequences are some of the highlight 
-	Some very unique visual designs 
-	Interesting premise of altered history 
-	Great shooting and gunplay, weapons feel stellar

-	Despite the same colour palate for its levels there is a unique design and world here 

[b] The Bad [/b] 
-	Enemies can feel bullet sponging and throwing waves at you just to add the difficulty
-	AI not very bright and uneven at times
-	Stealth sections while well design is brought down because of the AI being quite dumb in this section

[h1] The Summary [/h1]
 
[b] Gameplay 7 [/b] – Solid shooting and some well thought out level design brought down by enemy AI and weak stealth sections 

[b] Graphics 8 [/b] – Its honestly quite a looker for a 2014 game. Some of the environments are very well design and quite gorgeous to look at giving it personality

[b] Sound 8 [/b] – The voice acting is really good especially for Frau Engel and BJ monologues. The music is another stellar moment executing it to perfection with its epic moments and quite ones as well. The German voice acting adds to that immersion 

[b] Story 9 [/b] – A surprise for me as I am used to Wolfenstein series having a generally cheesy story with good gunplay. Here the story is solid, heartfelt and well written. It’s also surprising that it touches some really tough topics and overalls handle it with a lot of care giving it a strong cinematic feel.
   
[h1] The In Depth review [/h1]

2014 Wolfenstein New Order, is a great reimagining and reboot of the classic Wolfenstein that I so fondly remember from the early 90’s. At times it literally feels like a blast from the past, with the way its story is told through solid gunplay, game design and BJ feeling remarkably lost in this new world rule by the Nazi regime. It still retains a lot of the classic satisfying shooting from ID software iconic Doom and Wolfenstein series while at the same time being infused with a stronger emphasis on narrative and immersion.
  
Machinegames I believe did an exceptional job bringing this franchise back from obscurity and in a way giving proper respect to the character and franchise that ID software created. You play again once more as the iconic William “BJ” Blaskowizc again battling his way through the ever advancing Nazi regime and his nemesis General Strasse aka "Deathshead". The growing technological advancement of the Nazi military has turn the tide of the war forcing the allies to go on a full frontal assault of Deathshead lab which unfortunately goes awry sending our wounded BJ stuck in a coma for fourteen years in a mental asylum of sorts. Awakening in 1960, BJ is brought through a rude and violent awakening where the world is now being rule by the Nazi’s and the allies have lost the war. Along the way, he meets some strong supporting cast that help him on his journey in fighting the Nazi regime. The cast are enlightening and entertaining bunch from Wyatt naïve but goofy self or Fergus a wise cracking Scottish to Christine the tough as nails stoic leader leading the resistance to Anya BJ love interest to name a few. It helps that the writing is quite entertaining and heartfelt making the story quite profound at times. Some of the biggest highlight is the delivery of the story which is really quite a surprise for this franchise and the world building is astounding. What elevates this game even more are the villains, both Deathshead and Frau Engel are some of the biggest highlights of the game with their menacing carefree attitude at eradicating everything that is not perfect. The voice actors who play them give a really great performance.

The gunplay is still as satisfying as ever and feels remarkably weighty. Its gloriously satisfying to carry around two assault rifles or shotguns and blow away at your enemies. It helps that the level design is really quite good, varied and inventive. From the London Nautica base with its space observatory, to urban cityscapes, a destroyed bridge, a submarine and even the moon. The addition of cover is interesting but this game rewards you for aggressive offensive play which is the most fun when you are running around blowing everything to smithereens. The cover mechanic though runs really smoothly which is quite surprising to me. Despite the lack of weapon variety, the gunplay never got old and still really retains a lot of ID’s iconic FPS moments. There are also added stealth options of you eliminating commanders so that you face less enemies. I was surprised to learn that Wolfenstein originally started as a stealth game when I was reading up on the franchise. This added stealth section is a nice Easter egg for people who knows Wolfenstein history. However these are some of the weaker sections of the game. The AI is uneven at times, and is especially obvious during the stealth sections where they are not the brightest lightbulb in the room. Which is a shame since the gunplay is so good. Enemy variety is there from various type of infantry to giant human Soldaten robots to Panzerhounds but at the end of the day it becomes a giant shooting galore which is something Wolfenstein continues to excel at. It’s sad though the AI kind of brings down that satisfaction a tiny wee bit.

Wolfenstein honestly shines because of how satisfying the shooting is and how good the delivery of the story is. BJ monologues are remarkably heartfelt in exploring regret, guilt and anguish. The scenes are so well acted they might have just made a movie as the voice work is excellent. There are definitely a lot of inspiration it draws from films like Inglorious Basterds and even to some extent Schindler's List when it starts delve into tough topics. The weird humor and heartfelt moments are overall handle really well providing a fine balance of entertainment. They even added a bit more of replay value by adding choices within the game. [b]DISCLAIMER:[/b] This game is currently [u]unplayable[/u] on graphics cards released 2016 (AMD 400 series and nVidia 10 series) and later. On my RX 5700, I experienced screen tearing, 35-45 fps and crashes after almost every cutscene. No fix, including changing settings or changing the Steam game id did helped me at all.

I had an old R9 390X on hand, so I was able to play the game normally. Because the problem emerged over 2 years after the release of the port, I did not consider it in my review.

[h1]The Nazis Won[/h1]

You are Brad Pitt impersonator [strike]Chad McChadingson[/strike] William J. Blaskowitz, and you have just woken up after a 16 year coma. The year is 1960, and the Nazis won the war. Armed with nothing but heavy munitions, your chad-physique and a hot nurse gf, you seek out the resistance and beat back the Nazis.

The story and atmosphere are over average, and the plot was interesting enough to keep me engaged, but it’s definitely not a revolution in video game storytelling, nor is it trying to be. It can be dumb at times, but it’s “fun” dumb. “Let’s go to the Nazi moon base!”. What ends up carrying the story and characters is the atmosphere. The game portrays the counterfactual of a Nazi controlled world as a grey, cruel, slightly green tinted place, which is contrasted with the resistance’s warm headquarters (spoilers, you meet up with them). It feels like you have something to fight for, and even if some of the dialogue is played out at times, I was engaged enough to care about a lot of the characters. Of course, if the game is all cutscenes and no gameplay, why wouldn’t it just be a movie?

[h1]Use More Gun[/h1]

When actually playing the game, you’ll notice that Wolfenstein draws a lot of inspiration from the games released a few years prior. The stealth mechanics resemble Dishonored without powers, and the shooting resembles Bioshock: Infinite, with similar gun archetypes, enemy silhouettes and enemy types. However, that’s not to say that Wolfenstein is a clone of either of these games. It manages to blend stealth and action in its own unique way.

When approaching a section, there’s often a stealth component. For many games, stealth and action are separate, but in Wolfenstein, stealth augments action by giving you an opportunity to “scope out” a section before choosing when to engage, and rewarding you for doing so. You can assassinate Nazi commanders to prevent reinforcements, get to a vantage point and kill smaller enemies. The stealth gameplay doesn’t allow for much skill expression as it’s more about finding the hatch or side-alley than being a “mechanically good” stealth player. I don’t think that’s bad though, because it encourages you not to reload saves. The most fun I had in the game was sneaking in a tunnel or vent, overhearing racist Nazi guard conversations, then emerging on the high ground with a laser turret to blast them away!

As for the shooting, it’s basic, but by no means inadequate. You can single and dual wield weapons which are supposed to add an element of choice, do I need accuracy or damage? However, the shooting similarly doesn’t allow for all that much skill expression. The enemies have one crit area at their head, but because of how big their models are, and how slowly they move, the shooting doesn’t have all that much skill expression. Why would I single wield if even double wielding is enough to headshot? This is also where my biggest criticism of the game lies.

The best difficulty is “Bring it on”. On the highest difficulty, Über, I found that while the raw difficulty went up, it wasn’t adding a fun experience. You can win so long as you play around with your Laser ARs and Rockets, but by doing so the game devolves into standing next to power stations waiting for enemies to go around a corner. This is where the lack of skill expression in shooting hurts the game, because ideally you’d want to kite enemies while blasting them with shotguns, but if you try that in game you'll just get stat checked by anything but the weakest enemies. It’s for that reason I think that playing the game on “Bring it On'' is the best experience because stealth is still relevant (you can’t just Blaskowitz through everything), but the action doesn’t become a tedious game of peek-a-boo. A way to make the shooting more fun would be to increase mobility on both sides, while adding more vitals to outposition your Nazi opponents.

Overall, I really liked Wolfenstein though and recommend it if you want to play a fun Narrative-based FPS. I think newer games do what Wolfenstein does but better, but even then it’s still a good and fun game to play.

P.S. If you want to replay the game with another (Wyatt/Fergus) timeline, do NOT click “New Game” in the main menu, because that will wipe all your progress with the character you already played with. Instead, go to chapter selection and go to the other timeline from there. Thank me later. :)

Also, the Nazi-themed collectables and German parody songs are a nice touch.

Intense gunplay, but it is marred by stealth sections, which feel forced at best and don't blend well with the bombastic elements of the gunplay.

But overall, the voice acting, the writing and even the gameplay bring a powerful package that you should not miss out on.

[h1]So Good That Playing It Now Brings Tears To My Eyes.[/h1] I don't know what the hell happened with this game, let alone why the later sequels couldn't live up to it, but dear God is this one of the best revivals in the games industry.

They took Wolfenstein, a series all about killing Nazis, and genuinely made a story that is as antifascist as you can imagine. From its diverse cast of characters, the deliciously evil villains, the jaw dropping set pieces (you liberate a concentration camp and then fight Nazi robots on the moon, who does that?!) Every 10 minutes or so, you're seeing something that you just wouldn't see in any other game. It's disturbing as hell at times though, the story doesn't pull its punches with the subject matter after all.

Beyond this, the levels are satisfying to explore and replay thanks to two separate timelines that allow you to either hot wire or lock pick your way through hidden areas. The level design isn't quite as nonlinear and maze like as boomer shooter fans would prefer, unfortunately, but the game makes up for this in other ways. Namely, the sick ass soundtrack by Australian badass Mick Gordon which compliments your Reich slaying crusade extremely well, whilst also complimenting the more somber moments as well. The gunplay is also fantastic thanks to being able to dual wield everything known to man and a small touch of science fiction weapons that FPS fans will drool over.

It really is the perfect storm, and I hope to God that the next Wolfenstein is more like this instead of what the sequels have become...

[b]A refresing modernification of the series.[/b]

In short Wolfenstein: The New Order is story-driven FPS with sneaking and explosive action. The game is set mostly in 1960's Nazi-Europe. I played the game once through, took about 16h on über difficulty. Completed missing achievements in 3h. I have played both Wolfenstein 3D and Return the Castle Wolfenstein, but didn't know about 2009 version of Wolfenstein until after playing this one. 

If Doom(2016) is a near-perfect upgrad to 90's shooters, Wolfenstein: The New Order brings the shooters from 99-04 to modern times. If you remember games like [b]No One Lives forever, Soldier of Fortune, Return the Castle Wolfenstein and Codename Eagle[/b], this is something very similar. Healthpacks and armor from the 90's era are still here, but so are the varying levels, scifi/fantasy settings and somewhat serious tone from the later era. Skill tree is there to remind us that this isn't just a graphics update but a part of an an evolution of a genre.


What W: TNO does right is the core mechanic. In First person shooters the shooting should be fun or atleast enjoyable. That hasn't been the case in quite many games in recent years. Most CoD4 look-a-likes have failed to understand that there should be something of a feedback from shooting people in games. I'm not talking about XP or pop-ups but a feeling that I'm doing something violent to another (virtual)person. So after I had charged through the trenches of the first level with dual wielded assault rifles, I took a long look behind me and saw a bloody mess. Although the gun sounds are somewhat lacking in this game, the effects on enemies made me feel like I was shooting guns, not playing laser tag. 

Another thing W:TNO does right is it's skill mechanic. Although the skill mechanic is mostly boosting your existing abilities, it works like a charm and it rewards you for playing in a certain way. Unlike many other games with similar mechanics, you get certain skills for doing certain things. If you sneak, you unlock sneaking perks, and if you use explosive you unlock explosive perks. Progress towards skills is not lost on death, so it is relatively easy to obtain all skills during one playthrough.

The games atmosphere gets also an honorary mention. Although the plot revolves around the goofy idea of Nazi Germany winning world war 2 using robotic dogs, the plot stays dark from start to finish. The story sounds absurd but the game stays true to the idea. The world and it's characters act like it's the most natural thing and there exists only handful of moments where the game implies that this might be ridiculous. So the game isn't making fun of itself but let's the player decide if he takes it seriously or not. 

The story relies heavily on characters and they are very well built. Most of the characters remain memorable even after just a short introduction. Enemies instill fear with their actions and your friend have their own reasons to keep on the fight. The soundtrack adds to the atmosphere though it isn't exactly true to the timeframe.

There are also some features to critique. The game is easy.  I usually pick the medium difficulty with games but in this case I changed to the hardest after 1 hour of playing and found that equal to medium in many other games. I barely had to replay any parts because there was plenty of armor and health around even on the hardest difficulty. The intelligence and the amount of enemies is also lacking so the game is easy almost to the finish line. Then again I like the fact that the difficulty only ramps up enemies damage, they mostly die quite easily on harder difficulties too atleast if you aim for the head.

The graphics are decent. The game worked just fine for me and looked good enough, but the inconsistency of graphics affected the experience some what. Forced depth of field, no simple AA-setting and some blurry textures made the game occasionally look unnecessarily ugly. Most levels where colorful and the level design was good enough for most of the time. There has been reported serious performance issues with AMD GPU's and the game has  frame-caps so do some research before buying if you think these might affect you.

So it's a fun shooter with a decent storyline. Sure it's not the game of the decade, but well worth the 7 euros it costs these days. If you're not into FPS games, this hasn't got anything radically new in it for you to try it. If you happen to like single player FPS-games, this is a must buy.

I was very surprised by Wolfenstein: The New Order. I expected an average to above average game, but it ended up being my game of the year (so far!). It’s hard to describe how much I enjoyed it but I will try.

Story wise it’s solid. There’s a great cast of characters that you meet throughout the 15 hour campaign. Each has their own story and their own place in the game world. Even the main protagonist BJ, is a much more fleshed out character than his previous depictions in the Wolfenstein games. Also, the cutscenes are incredible. They blended so well into the gameplay and gave me the impression I was watching a film.

In terms of gameplay, this is where Wolfenstein TNO shined the brightest. Every weapon in the extensive arsenal is fun to use, seriously. The weapon sounds, the destruction of the environment and the pure carnage that you can cause is unforgettable. Almost every weapon has alternate firing modes for mixing up the gunplay and making it more than just an average point and click FPS. Dual wielding originally seemed like an unnecessary novelty, but is actually a lot of fun that adds EVEN MORE variety to the way you can play (ex. one assault rifle can shoot rockets while the other fires full auto). Shooting enemies can pop heads, blast off armour, and generally shows a very detailed level of damage. Throughout almost every level there are multiple paths to choose. Because of this, most encounters can be approached with stealth or a more aggressive route.

Wolfenstein the New Order is easily in my top five games of all time. That’s not something I expected in this day and age (especially with all the crap I’ve played lately). This game is a big deal for me and I hope that others can appreciate it as much as I did, because it really deserves the limelight.

One of my biggest regrets is choosing to not complete this game sooner. I've had it for three years, started it multiple times and branched out into both paths, and yet I never finished it. Luckily, I decided to power through the game completely and now I realize why this game gets praised so highly. While I'm not sure I would say it's on par with last year's [i]DOOM,[/i] this game is extremely well made and deserves the recognition it gets.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

I don't think I need to explain how awesome the setting is for this game. Well, not in this category anyway. But overall the game is gorgeous to look at and it has an amazing atmosphere. One thing I particularly loved was how varied the chapters were, from being underwater in a U-Boat to being all the way up on the moon. Each chapter stood out from one another and stayed interesting from start to finish. The game's atmosphere is top-notch, as I said before, and you could feel the Nazi's terrifying omnipresence in the safest places. The graphics themselves look very good for the most part. At times the textures were a little dated, but it can be excused because of how great everything else is.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

I had a blast playing through this game. The combat was fluid and satisfying, and it kept me on my toes. Thanks to the game's varied settings, each mission had something special to it that kept the game fresh and interesting. Something I was quite shocked that I enjoyed was the game's stealth mechanics. They're as basic as stealth mechanics can get, but they flow quite nicely with the frantic, fast-paced shooting [i]Wolfenstein[/i] is known for. I had just as much fun stabbing Nazis in the back as I did shooting them in the face, and I was pleasantly surprised by this. The major complaint I have with the gameplay, however, is in the form of its boss fights. Boss fights in shooters aren't usually that good, but this game's bosses in particular felt even more tedious. Playing this after finishing [i]Binary Domain,[/i] another game with lackluster bosses, I realized that at least [i]Binary Domain's[/i] boss battles were exciting to some degree. With this game, all I did was shoot some rockets and some lasers and then [i]BOOM[/i] they're dead. They also disrupted the pacing and made my experience more aggravating than it should've been. Aside from that, however, this game is a joyride to play.

[h1]Story[/h1]

The thing that makes [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i] stand out from other shooters is how compelling the main story is. It's definitely the highlight of the game, at least for me. Some people might think the emotional bits and the dream sequences break the mood, but [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfEBrCQ8VCI]Writing on Games made a fantastic video analyzing the story.[/url] To sum up his video, the game isn't about "taking the world back from the Nazis" because they're omnipresent. They've already won. [i]The New Order[/i] focuses more about the people surviving within it. I wholeheartedly agree with him, and it works extremely well in this game. The side characters and even B.J. himself are very flawed and two-sided, and they feel a lot more human the most video game characters do. It makes the game's extremely detailed world all the more fascinating. And let me tell you, this game is DETAILED. On top of all the little newspaper clippings and audio logs you can look into, they've even gone as far as to make [b]fake pop music you can listen to in-game[/b] to show how much influence the Nazis have. I could go on and on about this stuff, but unfortunately I can't do so here. The only problem with the story, in my opinion, was how forced the ending was. I knew it was going to be a trilogy from the start, but the way the cliffhanger was done here felt so unbelievably forced it slightly ruined the experience for me.

[h1]Audio[/h1]

First off, the voice acting in this game deserves quite a bit of credit. I was really impressed with everyone's performances, even the gravelly-voiced B.J. Blazkowicz. It really gave the characters more depth and emotion. As for the music, I didn't think it was particularly noteworthy until the last few chapters, where the music became kickass and I found myself being more pumped up than normal to kill some Nazis. There really isn't much else to say here aside from kudos to the voice actors for their amazing performances here.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]

This game does have branching paths. Seems interesting enough, but unfortunately they hardly differ from one another. There isn't really any point to playing through the game multiple times unless you really really enjoyed it, and I'm a little disappointed by that.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

To conclude, although [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i] does have some glaring flaws, I can't deny the game was a thrilling experience from start to finish. I'm looking forward to the sequel, and if it irons out the shortcomings of this game, there's a very good chance it could end up being one of my all-time favorite shooters. For $20, I absolutely recommend this game. It's not on par with [i]DOOM[/i] in my opinion, but it's still an extremely fun title that I'm sure will keep you entertained as much as it did for me. Definitely one of the highlights of this generation.

[h1]Game Review[/h1]

[i]"Kicking some Nazi butts."[/i]

[b]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/b] is the new installment in the iconic Wolfenstein series. In this game, you will have to defeat the Nazi forces once more. In it, you take control of Captain B.J. Blazkowicz, an American War Hero and the last hope to defeat the monstrous Nazi regime, which is packed with tons of foes, including Super Soldiers and Nazi Robots.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

For me the gameplay is near perfection, it is definitely where this game really shines. Everything about the shooting mechanics works like a charm. It really gives you the feel of playing an old-school First-person shooter, while being up to today standards. You have a nice variety of weapons to cause massive mayhem and destruction. Yet you can also try to go stealth which also is very well done, but the shooting in this game is so awesome that you probably wont go stealth. You also can dual-wield some weapons, which feels awesome too. Also enjoyed the boss battles a lot, one of them gave me a pretty good challenge. The AI was nothing exceptional though, sometimes during stealth sections they were pretty blind. Nevertheless, it is a really exceptional game gameplay wise, except for 2 things that bugged me. The laser cut sections, which got lame after a while into the game and the perk system since it is very bland. I wished they had put a little more effort in it but oh well...

[b]Story[/b]

The story is also very competent. It is very interesting to see this "what if nazis won World War 2" approach. Plus the game has tons of extremely interesting characters with great writing to support it, which make the story of this game work incredibly well. An excellent surprise.

[b]Graphics and Performance[/b]

Graphically this game is nothing special for a next-gen game. Yet the visuals work extremely well, with some amazing level design and scenarios, from underwater sections to the moon (yea you heard it right, the fricking moon). Unfortunately the performance was not very smooth as in all games that run in id Tech 5 engine. Played it on Max Settings around 50 fps at 1440x900 res in my medium specs rig (see my profile for specs), with the game having some noticeable breaks, but nothing that ruined my experience. The game comes packed with plenty of settings to tweak, so you probably wont have a problem playing it properly.

[b]Longevity[/b]

Longevity is nice for a single-player only First-person shooter, but definitely nothing impressive. I completed it in about 10 hours on normal difficulty, but I missed tons of collectibles, so I will probably replay it soon. It also as an interesting story choice right at the beginning of the game that affects the game, story-wise, so it can be played 2 times due to some interesting differences in the playthrough.

[b]Music and Sounds[/b]

The Sound department in this game is near perfect. All sounds felt right - gunfire, explosions, everything basically. Also the voice acting is top notch as the soundtrack. A really well done job in the sound department.

In one phrase: a fantastic FPS.

It gets pretty heavy though. It's obviously set in a universe where the Nazis definitively won WWII and have advanced technology; even if you spend most of the game eviscerating the scumbags, it really doesn't hold back on the regime's brutality. Sometimes you don't even have the upper hand. The game is also unflinching when it comes to BJ's behavior and emotions, which can be explicit. In other words, it's intense for a gonzo sci-fi shooter.

Portraying the Nazis as anything other than cartoon villains is a difficult balance to strike, especially if you're writing an Axis victory story. This is just my opinion, of course, but I feel that TNO manages to mostly strike this balance, given that the actual Nazi characters you see are presented as both [i]human[/i] and [i]really, really screwed up[/i]. Evil, basically, except that evil has become the new standard of good in their society.

On that note, the writing and worldbuilding in general is great, and for an FPS it's excellent. Its sense of style is scrumptious too: it's quite a cinematographic game, but not in a way that detracts from the game itself. The only criticism I would have is that BJ's monologues can get a little overwrought, even for this game.


Gameplay-wise, TNO is an example of successful modernization of a game series: it successfully keeps the spirit of Wolfenstein while enhancing and adding onto the experience. Movement and shooting feel like Wolfenstein 3D and a modern shooter had a baby, a very satisfying baby. The fact that stealth is as viable as it is hearkens back to the [i]original[/i] Wolfenstein games of the early 1980s, which were top-down stealth games. That's pretty cool, really.

Mind you, it's still an FPS. You're still essentially doing nothing but plugging Nazis full of holes or slitting their throats; it's just a more meaningful experience now.

Oddly enough, this game about being the toughest brickhouse of a man to have ever lived provided me a moment of introspection. As William walks through the sewers of Berlin, he can hear some chatter from the residents in the houses above. People talking about how the mold that seems to persistently grow on the concrete was made by the various anti-nazi terrorist cells. A nosy neighbor trying to report a boy trying on his mother's lipstick to the police. A man telling his wife about his brother's travels in China, and how there's going to be good business opportunities in Beijing once it's rebuilt. Another man telling his wife in hushed whispers about how the neighbors were disappeared in the middle of the night, and his wife telling him to keep his head down and stay vigilant for anyone else who might be subversive. All of this makes me wonder... who would I be in this kind of setting? What if an authoritarian government got their hands on some hyper-advanced tech and conquered the world with it? Who would I be in that situation? Sure, I'd like to think that I would be like B.J., stepping up and fighting back when the world needed a one-man-army, but would I really? Or would I just be that man, talking about business prospects in newly rebuilt Beijing? Would I be that woman, telling her husband to keep his head down? If I had the choice, would I fight, or would I slip into compliance to save my own skin? Just something to think about.
This game presents a convincing argument that the best way to improve the world is to remove Nazis from it. I agree with this thesis.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a First Person Shooter where you play a guy who wakes up in 1960 following a bodged job back when the war was still on, only to find that the Nazis won the war and that simply won't do. So you pick up some guns and you set out to obliterate as many Nazis as you can.

It is very much story driven, and my goodness what a story. The writing is superb, the dialog is exceptional and the voice acting is wonderful. 

The combat itself is a lot of fun. It is smooth, the variety of weapons is suitable. The cover system is good too. You fight everything from your bog standard soldiers to giant walking Nazi mechwarriors with a range of guns and explosives. Sometimes, you get the option to go stealth - that is, sneak upon the enemy and stealth kill them instead. Of course, you are very welcome to go in guns ablazing if that is more your style.

Wolfenstein is a good looking game, and it sounds great too, featuring an awesome soundtrack. The animations I found most impressive - the characters really come out well, helped by some cracking voice acting.

I haven't touched a First Person Shooter in quite some time, but this one quite simply blew me away. It is great to see one being built solely for the purpose of providing a solid single player experience, and here it does not disappoint.

Highly, HIGHLY recommended, even if you are not a big FPS player.

Two aspects. The gameplay and the writing.

[b]The Gameplay[/b]

Unexpectedly, Wolfenstein: New Order is NOT the spiritual sucessor of ye olde 90s shooters. That would be the new Doom. Wolfenstein is in fact an odd breed of a tactical shooter. If that sounds crazy, let me put it in the following perspective.
I've beaten this game twice. Both times - on the Über difficulty, in which you die pretty much as quick as regular enemy soldiers.

[i]The first time around[/i] I played it like a madman, throwing myself from one corner of the room to the opposite, unloading dual-wielded shotguns right in the Führer's face and dying every five seconds like the Bulletstorm adept that I am. I would scold the game for lack of stealth segments, frequent impossibility to hide anywhere and the unbelievably brutal final phase of the final boss.

[i]The second time[/i], three years later, I played it again, this time slowly and cautiously, carefully picking right weapons for right situations, capitalizing on weaknesses of different enemy types, constantly reevaluating the combat situation and glueing myself to cover at all times. And the game shone. Thanks to the ingenious idea of special leaning mode, not dependant on you being in cover, you gain control over your whole body, allowing you to lie down or stand on tiptoes if you need to shoot below or over an obstacle. Suddenly, I discovered a lot more opportunities for stealth than before. I learnt to dispatch certain enemies quickly and efficiently and anticipate how the AI is going to react to my actions. As a result, I would always have to check whether I'm actualy playing on Über - so much easier it got.
You may say that I just got gud. That might be true, but only partially. Now it is clear to me that at its core Wolfenstein favors a thoughtful approach to combat and punishes gung-ho attitude. Nowhere it's as clear as in the AI which tends to wait you out if you conceal yourself and then simultaneously opens fire from all cannons once you rear your head.

The Wolfenstein reboot is often compared to the Doom reboot with the latter usually considered to be superior in the way of combat mechanics. That seems entirely unfair to me, because these two games have extremely different approach to combat: Doom stimulates aggression while Wolfenstein encourages caution. And it is very much fun to play.

[b]The Writing[/b]

Oh... This one is odd too. It's neither here nor there.

[i]On the one hand[/i], Nazis seems to be humanized a lot through environmental storytelling (portraits of commanders used for target practie, cute home-sewn aprons hanging around) and letters (some of which are awesome Apocalypse-Now-ish takes on Wehrmacht's expansion across the world). [i]On the other hand[/i], all the Nazis Blazkowicz meets are either sadists or cowards, or nacissists with the exception of the U-boat captain,I suppose. When in combat, they sound absolutely hysterical, not shouting so much as howling orders at each other. The biggest sadist and narcissist is the main antagonist, who is just comically evil. He sounds ominous and deranged and spews slogans throughout all of your long fight with him.

Another example. [i]On the one hand[/i], the merry band of resistance fighters are all very human-like with normal sets of reactions and curious attitudes. [i]On the other hand[/i], they all fall into some or other boring trope. Especially the mystical-judaic-tech specialist. It's so dumb at times. And at other times it's very natural and touching. 

[i]The only real star[/i] here is the protagonist himself. A hulking phlegmatic heap of meat and muscle with enough reflection to supplement his mayhem with poetic one-liners but not enough to let his feelings outside. The writers stroke a fine balance with him - and successfully so. It's a shame this balance was destroyed in the New Collossus where BJ Blazkowicz turned into a melancholical ruin which then suddenly became an optimistic action figure again.

Some people say New Order's style belongs to Magic Realism, but I think it belongs to the school of inconsistent writing. It feels like there were a few people working on a story and everyone tugged in a different direction. The result is very good compared to most other games, yet not good enough to go into textbooks on how to merge the tropes demanded by popular culture and the actual good literature.

In summa: play it. It's a highlight among shooters. And if you're thinking whether you should play the New Order or the New Collossus, just go with this one. It's purer and more focused on the world rather than characters as well as more balanced in gameplay.

PS
The final phase of the final boss is still a doozy, though.

PPS

This is the middle of the XXth century, every second country is playing the nationalistic card and every other one - the socialistic one. Is this represented in a game? Yes. In newspaper extracts you might or might not read. That's not enough for a portrait of an epoch.

Some perks required you to kill 2 enemies with a grenade which is easy enough, while others are kill enemies using the assault rifle from cover 80 times. I got the perk and the steam achievement, here’s the thing, less that 10% of people on steam have this achievement. Still you can play the game however you want but just not as OP as you would like.

The game settings are good, a real techno brutal feel of the Nazi regime. All right angles and white stone, no room for frivolity or colour. There is definitely this neo-traditional vibe around it. What did creep into my history radar for inaccuracy was Frau Engels, who is a high ranking Nazi scientist. That’s an alt history anachronism because the Nazis did not like women in the workplace.  Okay we can wave that off because this isn’t a realistic game but then be careful a lot of things in this game can be explained away as being ‘not realistic’. Sooner or later you end up in the resistance in Berlin and the mood is a little weird. It’s a bit of a celebration of the arts but it feels too much on the nose, like it has to be different because we need to directly oppose the nazis. Also what begins to get a little wearing is BJ’s monologues, every now and again he inserts some sort of folksy story that drones on for a while. There is a reason why Gianni Matragrano can make BJ so memeable.

Now when it comes to the second half, when you go into the Berlin Catacombs, that’s when the game begins to fall apart. Now remember how I said using the silenced pistol was tricky? That problem now extends to a lot more enemies and weapons. The enemy shotgun guys are exceptionally tough, you can unload entire clips of assault rifle directly into their face and they can still easily hit you in return and not die. This starts extending to the regular troops closer to the end of the game. Overall all enemies become tankier bullet sponges and it becomes a chore to take them down. They also have amateur hour grade staggering poses that make it look as if they go to die and then suddenly they can start fighting again, it’s irritating. Your arsenal is expanded but one thing I kept finding was that there wasn’t a great gun to use in those situations. There wasn’t a troubleshooter gun you could use. By the end of the game I was using dual laser rifles a lot to deal with most enemies. It has range and punch which I found to be a common problem. Also by the end of the game you have so many weapons that it becomes very difficult to pick out weapons from the weapons wheel in the middle of a fire fight. It’s also about now you begin to wonder how the Nazi laser weapons are practicable? They only hold enough charge for 20 seconds of full fire tops. Yet you cannot seemingly reload them except at special points. The big mechs I can understand but not the regular guys, they don’t have power sources for this. How are these weapons practical for the battlefield? In the moon level they have batteries and suddenly this feels like the ammo shift from Mass Effect 1 to 2. Again this game isn’t realistic, but it still makes you ask too many questions.

The Moon level was a decent level but aside from that the rest felt awful, the scenery got in the way, it was difficult to move around in and it was filled with bullet sponge enemies. Gibraltar bridge was awful, it was a constant turkey shoot and the platforming was awful. Also, why drop me off at one side of the bridge when you could have dropped me off closer? Your buddy literally does this at the end of the second half making the reason for the level completely moot. Skipping ahead to the final boss fight, it’s a stinker. The first boss is a gimmick boss while the second bit is a running around exercise and trying not to be hit. The final section is a classic bulletsponge section. I empty my dual laser rifles and empty all my rockets into the boss. Game over, I skip the cutscene because I really don’t care for the slow and overly sentimentally saturated storytelling.

Also the other thing that made me stop and take a minute was the underlying story. The idea of secret Jewish technology bunkers is awful. Again it raises too many questions. Why are there bunkers? Why isn’t this technology being used? Did nobody think that leaving tech around like this was a bad idea as any asshat could find them and subvert the technology? Also it’s such a direct confrontation with the Jewish issue in that it feels really cliché. This is a definite golem analogy but it’s implemented like a brick. Nothing fancy or slick like Superman which had no Jewish connotation save that of the golem, nah this vault had stars of David everywhere.

So there you have it. What you might not have got from this review was the games good qualities. It can be really fun to sneak around and make potshots but that doesn’t last. It becomes a grindy slog that stops being fun to play.

I am so anxious to review this game. Ladies and gentlemen, I think I have found a new favorite.
Being a testosterone filled man with deep-seated cravings for violence hard-coded into my DNA from my primal, dinosaur hunting ancestors I of course lose my mind when I come across something that's hardcore, violent, action-packed and overall manly. Wolfenstein: The New Order of course, does not let me down.
Starting off with the basics: Wolfenstein is a revisit of the classic shooter series of the same name, taking on the role of Captain B.J. Blazkowicz you start the game in a desperate final push against the German war machine in 1946 (this is an alternate timeline of our history, so don't be upset if the game isn't historically accurate). Wolfenstein has amazing gunplay, a good story that is much more gripping than I expected, excellent level design and all-around great variety. 
The gameplay is mostly focused on the shooting, as you can expect from a classic FPS revisit. The firearms have a steady and satisfying punch to them and enemies react appropriately when shot, making for some very nice gameplay. You also have the option to dual-wield most of the weapons in the game, firing two at once by holding down both mouse buttons increasing your overall damage per second but draining your ammo supply faster, but who cares? Manliness brotha. After each shootout the level is noticably affected by it, where most first-person shooters would leave a small handful of bodies and a few splashes of blood on the walls, Wolfenstein has great bullet-impact decals, destructable cover and very nice gore effects, making the area immediately after the slaughter look like it has been completely decimated by the shootout, again, making you feel like an unstoppable bad-@ss. 
However, the gameplay is not just restricted to you being an unstoppable killing force. You can also play with a more stealth-minded approach, using a silencer attachment to your pistol, satisfying melee takedowns and even being able to throw your knives for an instant and silent kill. The game is pretty adaptable and while the AI isn't too suited for stealth it still gets the job done well enough. There are four different skill-trees in the game that unlock perks for the player as the game progresses, but unlike most skill-tree based games there isn't some level-up system followed by going into the menu and selecting which perk you want, instead the perks are unlocked based on challenges such as X amount of stealth kills, X amount of pistol kills etc. so the player does not need to concern themselves with carefully selecting perks based on an in-game meta, instead simply play the game the way you like to play it, and everything else will fall into place. 
And before I get off the subject of gameplay, I want to make a quick sub-note: The enemies in this game just look badass. I love the Panzerhunds, the giant robot wolves with dagger-pointed teeth, and the frankenstein super-soldiers. Just. Wow, I feel my testosterone levels going berserk just thinking about it.
Level design in Wolfenstein is also very well made, with a fine balance between being fluid and controlled when it wants to be and switching to tight and intense when it needs to be. The transition between them is flawless, and each and every level has a unique design to them, making every chapter memorable and avoids being repetitive. In each level also are several hidden secrets, easter-eggs and collectables, creating a very welcome replay value to the game. I do indeed look forward to playing through again.
Now to the story: I wasn't expecting a huge impact with the story when I bought this game, similar to my expectations with Shadow Warrior. I was anticipating a mindless, shut-off-my-brain bullet and blood shower. But to my pleasant surprise Wolfenstein did in fact create a mighty well done story, not the best I've seen in any regard but surpassed all my expectations. B.J. Blazkowicz was taking part in the final push hoping to end the war in 1946, but events did not go according to plan and he and his team are captured and barely manage to escape, B.J. suffering a severe head injury in the process, putting him into a coma for 14 years. 1960, the war is over and the world is now under the iron-fist of the Third Reich, B.J. is in a vegitative state in a hospital in Poland when he is suddenly awoken by the scent of Nazi blood (MANLINESS). Seeing the world under control of the enemy he dedicated his life to destroy with extreme prejudice, he sets off to find any form of resistance to take the Reich apart piece by piece and take down his rival, a bitter little saurkraut known to most as Deathshead. 
While the story did exceed my expectations it also left a few disappointments as well. There were missed opportunities to create some very powerful and emotional moments that the game just slid over, but there are other times where the game doesn't shy away from doing just that. The story is surprisingly good, not exactly the most original of scripts but it was a very interesting idea and it did leave a memorable impact. Now that said, there are some sour-points with the story: Out-of-nowhere plot devices that are never mentioned again in the entire game, just serving no purpose other than to make the story advance. Sometimes the game will try to create some dramatic moments with some characters who are no better than cut-outs: Some examples include obvious love-interest girl, obvious trust-issues guy with a shady past, obvious Jewish guy who does everything to remind you that he's Jewish, obviously Hodor from Game of Thrones, and B.J. himself is for the most part just the heavily-muscled jarhead who always means well but will not let anything get between him and his mission. The ending was also very vague and left way too much unanswered, but there's DLC coming in so maybe that'll change, assuming you're not a cranky anti-DLC activist.

So to wrap all this up: Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game that met and exceeded all my expectations, it was a great joy to play beginning to end. I highly recommend Wolfenstein: The New Order.

Wolfenstein – The New Order is the latest instalment of the Wolfenstein Franchise.
I have been playing the Wolfenstein games since the Wolfenstein 3D era.
Someone who liked the previous games and the game style will absolutely love this new game.

Story:
As always you play "B.J." Blazkowicz but this time the story is set in an alternate reality. It’s 1960 and the Nazi’s won the war. The story of this game is well written and well-acted.

Game:
The game is only single player, there is no multi player. But that’s a good thing so the developers good focus all their attention to the single player game. Unlike a lot of games these days where single player is neglected.
It’s a fast action fps in true Wolfenstein style. Graphics and sound are impressive; it’s based on the id-tech engine (like Rage). The story unfolds via in engine cut scene’s. It’s impressive how much detail they put in the story telling.
The game can graphically be tweaked a lot, there are a of options that can influence you’re fps. So it’s important to read some of the guides if you have trouble running it.
I can confirm it also runs on ultra-wide screens 21:9 aspect ratio and a resolution of 2560*1080 without problems.
For those who have never played the original Wolfenstein 3D – the game that started the fps-genre – level 1 is hidden somewhere in the game.

This is a must for everyone’s game collection!
Highly recommended!
